headline: Public USB Ports Threat Analysis by FCC & CISA
summary: The FCC and CISA warn that free public USB charging stations expose mobile devices to juice jacking, where malicious hardware exploits dual-purpose power cables to siphon data and push malware. Understanding the data-line vulnerability and deploying proper hardware countermeasures are critical for travel security hygiene.

slides.title: That Airport Charging Station Is Watching You
slides.subtitle: Public USB ports combine power delivery with hidden data pipelines.
slides.body: You plug your dying phone into a convenient terminal at the airport gate, trusting it only provides electricity. In reality, that same physical slot can silently transmit your private files and install malicious code in seconds.
slides.deep_dive: Juice jacking exploits the inherent dual nature of standard USB architecture, which was originally engineered to carry both electrical current and digital data streams simultaneously over a single physical cable.
slides.key_fact: Public USB terminals can covertly bridge power delivery and data transfer.
slides.why_it_matters: Every unverified public charging port represents an unauthenticated entry point directly into your device's core operating system.

slides.title: Anatomy of a Juice Jacking Exploit
slides.subtitle: How charging stations double as covert data extraction nodes.
slides.body: When a user connects a smartphone to a compromised public kiosk, the hardware interface does not just route electrons. It handshakes with the device operating system, opening a bidirectional data tunnel disguised as a standard peripheral connection.
slides.deep_dive: Malicious actors modify airport or hotel charging kiosks by routing internal USB wires away from standard power blocks and into hidden minicomputers designed to interact with connected phones.
slides.key_fact: Standard charging cables combine power conductors with unprotected data wires.
slides.why_it_matters: Software prompts asking to 'Trust This Computer' can sometimes be bypassed or spoofed by highly modified hardware interfaces.

slides.title: The Three-Step Hardware Compromise
slides.subtitle: Tracing the exact path from wall outlet to total data exposure.
slides.body: The attack sequence unfolds silently within seconds of physical connection, requiring no user interaction beyond plugging in the cable.
slides.deep_dive: The exploit relies on the automated handshake protocols built into modern mobile operating systems designed for easy accessory pairing.
slides.key_fact: Compromise occurs automatically during the initial hardware handshake phase.
slides.why_it_matters: Users assume plugging in a cable is entirely passive, masking the active digital negotiation taking place underneath.

steps.title: Physical Bridge
steps.desc: The device connects to a modified port where data pins are wired to a hidden malicious host computer.

steps.title: Protocol Handshake
steps.desc: Operating system drivers negotiate connection parameters, establishing an active data tunnel alongside power flow.

steps.title: Data Extraction
steps.desc: Background scripts siphon cached credentials, media files, and device identifiers or inject malicious payloads.

slides.title: Inside the Standard USB Pinout
slides.subtitle: Why power and data travel down the exact same physical pathway.
slides.body: A standard USB connection contains multiple internal wires. While outer pins handle electrical power, the inner pins labeled D+ and D- manage high-speed data transmission.
slides.deep_dive: Because mobile devices use these exact data lines for both charging negotiation and file syncing, disabling data entirely can sometimes cripple fast-charging protocols unless properly managed.
slides.key_fact: Pins D+ and D- form the vulnerable data backbone of standard USB connections.
slides.why_it_matters: Hardware architecture that conflates energy delivery with data communication creates an inherent security paradox.

slides.title: The Fallacy of Blind Trust in Public Ports
slides.subtitle: Comparing naive charging habits with hardened operational security.
slides.body: Many travelers assume that as long as they do not unlock their screen, their device remains completely safe from external interference.
slides.deep_dive: Modern mobile operating systems handle background peripheral enumeration even while locked, opening potential attack surfaces if the physical data lines are left unshielded.
slides.key_fact: Locked screens do not automatically block low-level hardware enumeration.
slides.why_it_matters: Relying on software lock screens alone provides a false sense of security against sophisticated hardware-level attacks.
before_items: Plugging straight into public wall USB slots
Using standard multi-wire data cables everywhere
Assuming charging kiosks are passive power sources
after_items: Using AC wall adapters with standard power sockets
Carrying dedicated power banks for travel

slides.title: Establishing Hardware Defense-in-Depth
slides.subtitle: Isolating energy delivery from untrusted digital infrastructure.
slides.body: Protecting devices from juice jacking requires intercepting the physical data path before it ever reaches your device port.
slides.deep_dive: Hardware countermeasures like USB data blockers physically sever the internal D+ and D- wires inside the adapter shell, permitting only VBUS power to pass through.
slides.key_fact: Hardware-level physical isolation completely eliminates juice jacking risk.
slides.why_it_matters: Zero-trust principles applied to hardware ensure that external physical interfaces cannot be exploited.
right_items: Personal wall chargers plugged into AC

slides.title: Travel Security Hygiene Checklist
slides.subtitle: Essential protocols for engineers and tech leads on the move.
slides.body: Implement these rigorous travel habits recommended by cybersecurity authorities to safeguard your engineering hardware and sensitive repositories.
slides.deep_dive: Maintaining strict device hygiene during travel prevents corporate espionage and credential harvesting via compromised public infrastructure.
slides.key_fact: Proactive physical hygiene stops hardware-level endpoint compromise.
slides.why_it_matters: A single compromised device can jeopardize entire cloud infrastructure environments through leaked deployment keys.
items: Always use AC power outlets instead of direct USB slots
Carry a hardware USB data blocker for emergency charging
Never connect to unknown terminals without an intermediary power bank
